**Authors:** John Kulas, **Casey Osorio-Duffoo**, Mike DeFabiis, & Morgan Russell
**Role:** Second author
**Code:** [jtkulas/EngagementPaper](https://github.com/jtkulas/EngagementPaper) · [Engagement-Survey-Projects](https://github.com/heyimMIKE123/Engagement-Survey-Projects/tree/main/Measuring%20Invariance)

## The question

Over the past 15 years, organizations and researchers have increasingly *bought* survey responses from online panels such as Qualtrics and Prolific instead of recruiting volunteers. These panels are fast, but data quality questions remain. **Do people from purchased panels interpret a survey the same way as people who volunteered to take it?**

## Approach

We tested the measurement invariance of our 18-item engagement survey (see the [engagement paper](../engagement-paper/)) across samples, first three and then five:

1. Voluntary snowball sample (n = 232)
2. Qualtrics panel, cleaned (from 743 respondents)
3. Prolific panel, cleaned (from 785 respondents)
4. Qualtrics respondents flagged as careless
5. Prolific respondents flagged as careless

Using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis in `lavaan`, we compared configural, metric, and scalar models to see where the samples' responses diverged.

## My contributions

- Combined all three survey sources into one cleaned analysis data set, with documented sample sources and response dates
- Wrote and maintained the measurement invariance analysis in R Markdown

## Tools

R, `lavaan`, `tidyverse`, R Markdown, `papaja`, Git/GitHub
